description: We are a team of curious minds passionate about space exploration, physics, mathematics, and technology. For the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge, we aim to develop an interactive tool to help evaluate lunar landing sites using sunlight, terrain, and Earth visibility. We want to combine scientific research, coding, and creative problem-solving to support future lunar missions and make space exploration more accessible.
summary:
For our NASA Space Apps Challenge project, we developed an interactive, physics-based simulation game that puts players directly in the boots of a spaceflight crew member.

To address the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge, we built a hands-on experience that walks players through the full lifecycle of a mission. Instead of just pressing a launch button, players start on the launchpad—fueling the rocket and running critical safety inspections. Once cleared, real-world physics take over as players navigate through the layers of Earth’s atmosphere to reach orbit, ultimately charting a course toward the Moon and Mars.

This project matters because real space operations are often locked behind dense technical jargon and complex math. By turning actual pre-launch procedures and orbital mechanics into playable challenges, our game bridges the gap between entertainment and education. It gives anyone the chance to grasp the real science and teamwork required to explore our solar system, helping spark curiosity and inspire the next generation of space explorers.
details: Our project is an interactive space exploration game where you build your own spacecraft, fly to the Moon and Mars, and launch satellites out to the rest of the solar system. While we used Claude to help us out with the coding, all the actual ideas, game mechanics, and design came straight from our team. In the game, you have to carefully balance your fuel, budget, power, and spacecraft weight using real rocket physics and orbital mechanics—like the rocket equation, gravity, and orbital velocity formulas—to actually survive the trip. Our goal is to take intimidating subjects like astrophysics, advanced math, and complex moon orbits and turn them into something fun and easy to pick up by letting players experiment and see what happens when they tweak their rocket. We spent a lot of time figuring out how to keep the science realistic without making the gameplay feel like a boring textbook, creating a creative way for anyone to get hands-on with space engineering.
